cues.text: Orphaned by Smallpox
Born around 1656 near present-day Auriesville, New York, Tekakwitha had a Mohawk father and a Christian Algonquin mother.
Her mother had herself been captured and adopted into the Mohawk nation.
Her name meant roughly "she who bumps into things," and she lost both parents and an infant brother to a devastating smallpox epidemic at only four years old.
The same disease permanently scarred her face and severely damaged her eyesight.
Thereafter, she was self-conscious enough to cover her face with a blanket or shawl among strangers.
In the years that followed, she grew into a diligent and genuinely skilled worker among the women of her adoptive household.
Twice Refusing Marriage
Raised by an aunt and an uncle who had become a chief of the Turtle clan, Tekakwitha grew into a skilled, hardworking young woman.
She resisted with quiet firmness every attempt by her family to arrange a marriage for her — first at thirteen, and again more insistently at seventeen.
Her relatives and community found this refusal genuinely difficult to understand, given how thoroughly Mohawk social and economic life depended on the interdependence of married households.
A Chance Encounter, and Baptism
In 1675, confined indoors by an injured foot, Tekakwitha happened to be the only person present in her longhouse when a visiting Jesuit missionary called.
The missionary was Father Jacques de Lamberville, and the encounter opened the door to religious instruction she had, it seems, already been quietly drawn toward.
She was baptized the following Easter Sunday, 1676, taking the name Catherine — rendered in Mohawk as Kateri — after St.
Catherine of Siena .
Shunned for Her Faith
Kateri's baptism provoked hostility rather than acceptance from much of her own village, where she was mocked, accused of sorcery, and effectively treated as an outcast for her new faith.
To escape this pressure and practice her religion freely, she undertook an arduous journey in 1677.
She traveled some two hundred miles on foot to Kahnawake , a Christian Mohawk settlement near Montreal, where she finally found a community that shared and supported her convictions.
Her own uncle, though himself unconvinced by her new faith, quietly declined to forbid her the journey outright, a small mercy that made her escape to a more welcoming community possible at all.
A Vow and a Short, Devoted Life
At Kahnawake, Kateri made a private vow of perpetual virginity — an unusual and, to her Jesuit advisors, somewhat startling commitment for an indigenous woman of her era.
She devoted her remaining years to intense prayer, fasting, and penance, quickly earning the deep respect of both the lay community and the missionary priests.
They increasingly sought her counsel and admired the evident depth of her spirituality despite her failing health.

She was known among the community at Kahnawake for a joy that never seemed diminished by her physical suffering, and for a quiet, unforced holiness that drew even skeptical observers to reconsider their doubts about her.
Legacy
Kateri died at Kahnawake on 17 April 1680, only twenty-four years old, worn down by tuberculosis and years of austere personal penance.
According to later testimony, witnesses reported that after her death the smallpox scars that had marked her face appeared to vanish, and that she was left strikingly beautiful.
Beatified in 1980 and canonized in 2012 — the first Native American to be declared a saint — Kateri Tekakwitha remains patron of ecology and Native American Catholics.

Known ever since as the Lily of the Mohawks , she was a young woman whose quiet, unbending fidelity to a faith her own community initially rejected has drawn an entire continent's admiration across three and a half centuries.
Her cause continues to draw devotion from Native Catholics across North America who see in her life a bridge between their own heritage and the Christian faith she embraced at such cost.
